paragraphs: A model that generates plausible molecular configurations does not automatically explain how a molecule moves between them. This paper tackles transition path sampling: finding probable routes between two points on an energy landscape. Its aim is to reuse existing generative models for this task, avoiding the expensive training procedures that limit some current approaches.

The authors interpret candidate paths as trajectories of stochastic dynamics defined by a generative model’s learned score function. They apply this interpretation to denoising diffusion and flow matching models. Under these induced dynamics, finding a highly likely path is equivalent to minimizing the Onsager–Machlup action, a quantity that scores entire trajectories. This equivalence supplies an optimization objective for using pretrained models without additional task-specific training.

Demonstrations on the Müller–Brown potential and several fast-folding proteins produce diverse, physically realistic pathways. Tests on tetrapeptides also show successful sampling for systems absent from the generative model’s training data. These findings support repurposing models of molecular configurations for transition pathways, with the likelihood interpretation specifically tied to the dynamics the method constructs.
icml-2025-action-minimization-meets-gene.tldr: Pretrained molecular generative models can find transition pathways without additional training by minimizing an action defined by their induced dynamics.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive translation models offer efficient decoding, but their training can give them information unavailable when translating new text. In the approaches examined here, training sometimes supplies sampled words from the correct translation. At inference, those target words are unknown. The paper identifies this mismatch as an obstacle to realizing the models’ full translation performance.

Simply reducing the frequency of supplied target words to zero during training does not solve the problem cleanly: the authors report that this degrades performance. They instead propose adaptive end-to-end quantization alignment, which introduces a space designed to maintain semantic consistency. Training is adaptively aligned in that space without requiring target information as an input aid, bringing training conditions closer to actual use.

In the reported experiments, the framework outperforms most existing fully non-autoregressive models. It also reaches performance comparable to an autoregressive Transformer while delivering 17.0 times greater inference efficiency. The result suggests that addressing the information mismatch can preserve the decoding advantages of non-autoregressive translation while substantially improving its quality.
icml-2025-aeqa-nat-adaptive-end-to-end-q.tldr: AEQA-NAT aligns translation training with inference conditions, achieving autoregressive-comparable performance with substantially more efficient inference in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Temporal graph neural networks predict from systems whose relationships and features change over time. Explaining an individual prediction is difficult because both graph structure and event timing can matter. CoDy approaches this through counterfactual explanations: it searches for changes to the input graph that would affect a model’s prediction, making the model’s dependence on particular events easier to inspect.

The method produces explanations for individual instances and is designed to work independently of a particular temporal graph model architecture. It searches for counterfactual subgraphs using Monte Carlo Tree Search combined with heuristic selection rules. These rules use spatial relationships, temporal information, and the local impact of events to guide exploration through a large set of possible explanatory subgraphs.

Experiments compare CoDy with leading factual and counterfactual explanation methods. The authors report a 16% improvement in AUFSC+ over the strongest baseline. This provides empirical evidence that the guided search finds effective explanations in the tested settings, while retaining information about time that is central to interpreting predictions on dynamic graphs.
icml-2025-cody-counterfactual-explainers.tldr: CoDy explains temporal graph predictions by searching for counterfactual subgraphs using structural, temporal, and event-impact information.

paragraphs: Language model agents usually communicate by generating text for one another to read. This adds inference costs as agents and messages multiply, and converting internal representations into words can discard useful information. The paper investigates whether agents can communicate more efficiently by sharing intermediate activations directly.

The proposed operation is simple: pause one model at an intermediate layer, combine its activation with an intermediate activation from another model, and feed the combined result into the receiving model’s next layer. Computation then continues through decoding. The authors test several choices of the combining function. Their approach requires no additional parameters or data to apply this communication mechanism on new tasks.

Experiments cover multiplayer coordination games and reasoning benchmarks. The authors report improvements of up to 27% over natural-language communication across datasets, using less than one-quarter of the compute. These results support internal activations as a useful communication medium in the tested setups: agents can exchange information without paying the full cost of expressing and processing every message as text.
icml-2025-communicating-activations-betw.tldr: Sharing intermediate activations lets language model agents communicate with no added parameters or data and improves performance and compute efficiency in tested tasks.

paragraphs: A model can avoid harmful mistakes by declining to predict when uncertain. This paper identifies how that safeguard can be abused: an institution could deliberately lower confidence for selected inputs and use apparent uncertainty to justify denying services. The authors demonstrate Mirage, an attack that suppresses confidence in targeted regions while maintaining high predictive performance across the data.

Confidential Guardian addresses two parts of this problem. First, it checks calibration metrics on a reference dataset to detect confidence that has been artificially suppressed. Second, it uses zero-knowledge proofs of verified inference to establish that reported confidence scores were actually produced by the deployed model. These proofs protect proprietary model details while preventing providers from simply inventing confidence values.

The combination matters because accurate predictions alone do not establish honest confidence reporting. Calibration analysis examines confidence behavior, while cryptographic verification connects the reported scores to model execution. The authors report that the framework prevents the demonstrated misuse of cautious prediction, providing verifiable support for abstention decisions through both behavioral checks and verified inference.
icml-2025-confidential-guardian-cryptogr.tldr: Confidential Guardian combines calibration checks and cryptographic inference proofs to counter deliberate misuse of model uncertainty.

paragraphs: Boxplots summarize a dataset’s location, spread, asymmetry, and tails, making them useful for comparing distributions. This paper develops a differentially private boxplot so those summaries can be released with privacy protection. The challenge is to preserve the distributional information that makes the visualization useful while constructing it under differential privacy.

The authors establish different guarantees for different aspects of the plot. Location and scale estimates have optimal sample complexity, meaning their data requirements meet the relevant theoretical optimum. Estimates of skewness and tails are consistent, meaning they improve toward their targets as more data become available. The paper shows that a naive boxplot built from one existing private quantile algorithm does not always provide this consistency, and develops additional private quantile estimation results.

In simulations, the proposed visualization behaves similarly to a non-private boxplot and outperforms the naive private construction. An analysis of Airbnb listings also yields comparable analysis through private boxplots. Together, the theory and examples show why designing the visualization as a whole matters for preserving useful distributional summaries.
icml-2025-differentially-private-boxplot.tldr: The proposed private boxplot preserves useful distribution summaries with theoretical estimation guarantees and strong empirical similarity to ordinary boxplots.

paragraphs: Adapting pretrained graph neural networks to a succession of downstream tasks can require expensive fine-tuning. This paper investigates dataset distillation as a way to make graph continual learning more efficient and generalizable. The aim is to condense useful task information into distilled data while supporting several kinds of graph prediction.

The central tool is LIGHTGNTK, a lightweight graph neural tangent kernel. It combines a low-rank approximation of the graph Laplacian, constructed through Bernoulli sampling, with linear association inside the kernel. This design captures relationships involving both graph structure and features while allowing gradient-based dataset distillation. A unified subgraph anchoring strategy lets the framework accommodate predictions about whole graphs, individual nodes, and edges despite differences in their input structures.

Experiments on several datasets report state-of-the-art performance in graph continual learning scenarios. The contribution therefore combines an efficient kernel construction with a common treatment of multiple task types. The findings support this framework as a route toward more adaptive and scalable large graph models, rather than requiring a separate distillation formulation for each prediction level.
icml-2025-efficient-graph-continual-lear.tldr: LIGHTGNTK uses a lightweight graph kernel and unified subgraph anchoring to support efficient dataset distillation across graph continual learning tasks.

paragraphs: Optimizing a molecule against a protein target requires coordinating continuous spatial coordinates with discrete molecular types. Gradient guidance is attractive for steering generation, but discrete choices are difficult to guide directly, and separate guidance can make the two representations inconsistent. MolJO addresses this by placing them in a continuous, differentiable space derived through Bayesian inference.

This shared space allows guidance to act jointly across modalities. The framework also preserves SE(3)-equivariance, so its geometric behavior respects rotations and translations. A backward correction mechanism revisits a sliding window of recent optimization history. The authors use this mechanism to control the balance between exploring alternatives and exploiting promising solutions during optimization.

On CrossDocked2020, MolJO reports a 51.3% success rate, Vina Dock of -9.05, and SA of 0.78. Success rate exceeds that of the gradient-based counterpart by more than fourfold, while the reported “Me-Better” ratio is twice that of 3D baselines. Applications also include multiple objectives, R-group optimization, and scaffold hopping. These results support joint gradient guidance as a versatile strategy across the tested molecular optimization settings.
icml-2025-empower-structure-based-molecu.tldr: MolJO jointly guides molecular coordinates and discrete types in a differentiable Bayesian space, improving benchmark optimization results across several design settings.

paragraphs: Training an adaptive decision-maker often involves choosing among many tasks or randomized environments. Risk-averse methods emphasize difficult tasks, but identifying them through repeated policy evaluation can be expensive. This paper studies active task sampling, where a model predicts risk to help select training tasks without requiring intensive direct evaluation every time.

The authors formulate robust active task sampling as a secret Markov decision process and develop theoretical and practical insights for risk-averse settings. Their proposed method, Posterior and Diversity Synergized Task Sampling, combines posterior information with task diversity. The focus is on making task selection both useful for robustness and practical to implement, so the sampling process supports the training of adaptive policies.

Extensive experiments report stronger robustness on challenging tasks in both zero-shot and few-shot adaptation. These settings test adaptation with no task-specific examples or only a small number. PDTS also accelerates learning in certain scenarios. The speed benefit is therefore conditional, while the reported robustness improvements support actively selecting training tasks as a useful component of adaptive sequential decision-making.
icml-2025-fast-and-robust-task-sampling-.tldr: PDTS combines posterior information and task diversity to improve adaptation robustness, with faster learning in some tested scenarios.

paragraphs: Vision encoders supply feature maps used in tasks such as segmentation, object detection, depth perception, and vision-language understanding. Many widely used Vision Transformers, especially CLIP models, operate at fixed and relatively low image resolutions. That restriction makes it difficult to retain fine spatial details in the representations passed to downstream systems.

FeatSharp introduces a method for coherently upsampling the feature maps of low-resolution encoders at low computational cost. Its goal is to capture fine details that the original resolution would otherwise lose. The object being improved is the encoder’s feature representation, which makes the approach relevant to multiple tasks that consume those features.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness on core perception tasks and in agglomerative model training using RADIO. In the latter setting, the enhanced features provide richer targets for distillation, the process of training a model to reproduce another representation. These applications show two uses for sharper features: improving representations supplied directly to perception tasks and improving the supervision available when training another model.
icml-2025-featsharp-your-vision-model-fe.tldr: FeatSharp cheaply upsamples vision encoder feature maps to preserve finer details for perception tasks and model distillation.

paragraphs: This paper studies a theoretical version of learning to generate new valid examples. An adversary chooses a rule from a binary hypothesis class and supplies examples that satisfy it. The generator’s eventual goal is to produce new positive examples it has not already seen. The paper extends this setup to streams containing misleading examples.

The noise model is specific: the adversary inserts a finite number of negative examples into a stream of positive ones, and the generator does not know which entries are wrong. The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions for a hypothesis class to permit successful generation despite that corruption. They consider different constraints on how many distinct examples must be observed before generation becomes perfectly positive.

For finite and countable hypothesis classes, the authors find that generatability is largely unchanged by a finite number of noisy examples. This establishes a form of robustness for the theoretical generation problem. Its scope depends on eventual success and finite corruption; the result concerns whether reliable novel generation is possible under those conditions.
icml-2025-generation-from-noisy-examples.tldr: The paper characterizes when generators can eventually produce unseen positive examples despite finitely many hidden negative examples in their input stream.

paragraphs: Visual brain decoding connects recorded brain activity with images. Recent systems do this by aligning representations of brain signals with representations produced by image encoders. This paper asks whether the choice of image representation can improve that connection, especially when experiments present visual stimuli rapidly.

The authors introduce human-aligned image encoders into the decoding pipeline. Their hypothesis is that these encoders capture perceptual attributes better suited to the brain responses recorded during rapid presentations. The proposed change therefore concerns the image side of the alignment: a representation more closely matched to human perception may provide a better target for mapping brain activity.

Experiments support that hypothesis, with image retrieval accuracy improving by up to 21% over state-of-the-art methods. The authors also report consistent improvements across different EEG architectures, image encoders, alignment methods, participants, and imaging modalities. This breadth suggests that the encoder choice can benefit several decoding configurations. The stated gain concerns retrieving images from brain signals, and the 21% figure is the largest reported improvement rather than a uniform gain.
icml-2025-human-aligned-image-models-imp.tldr: Human-aligned image encoders improve visual retrieval from brain activity, with gains of up to 21% in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Importance sampling seeks to concentrate computation on data points that matter most to a model. Linear models have well-developed tools based on norms and leverage scores for making those choices. This paper extends those ideas to nonlinear models, where analogous notions of importance have been less developed.

The authors introduce an adjoint operator for a nonlinear map and use it to define generalized norm and leverage scores. Sampling according to these scores comes with guarantees for approximating the underlying nonlinear mapping. The intended parallel is with linear subspace embeddings: carefully chosen samples preserve useful properties of the larger mathematical object, allowing computations to use less data.

The scores have several stated applications. They can reduce the computational cost of training nonlinear models on large datasets, provide a mechanism for explaining model behavior, and help detect outliers. The paper supports these contributions with theoretical analysis and experiments across supervised learning scenarios. Its central contribution is therefore both a mathematical definition of nonlinear importance and evidence that this definition can guide useful data selection.
icml-2025-importance-sampling-for-nonlin.tldr: Generalized nonlinear norm and leverage scores enable importance sampling with approximation guarantees and applications to training, explanation, and outlier detection.

paragraphs: MindLLM translates fMRI signals into text while addressing two recurring difficulties: transferring across people and supporting different decoding tasks. Existing systems can struggle when a new participant’s input differs from the training data or when the desired output task changes. The model combines a dedicated fMRI encoder with an off-the-shelf large language model.

The encoder uses a neuroscience-informed attention mechanism that can accommodate different input shapes across participants. This supports a shared decoding approach across subjects. The authors also introduce Brain Instruction Tuning, which helps the model extract diverse semantic representations from brain signals. Together, these components address variation in both the incoming measurements and the kinds of meaning the model needs to express.

Across fMRI-to-text benchmarks, the authors report improvements over baselines of 12.0% on downstream tasks, 24.5% in generalization to unseen subjects, and 25.0% in adaptation to novel tasks. They also find that the attention patterns provide interpretable insights into model decisions. The results support broader reuse of a brain-to-text model across participants and tasks within the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-mindllm-a-subject-agnostic-and.tldr: MindLLM combines a flexible fMRI encoder with instruction tuning to improve brain-to-text decoding across subjects and tasks.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more output tokens creates opportunities for reasoning, but training must teach it to use that computation productively. This paper frames the allocation of test-time compute as a meta reinforcement learning problem. A long output stream is treated as several episodes, connecting reasoning to a balance between exploring possibilities and exploiting useful discoveries.

The authors propose cumulative regret as a measure of how effectively the model spends its computation. They show that regret can be minimized by combining a final binary success reward with a dense reward bonus based on information gain. Their measure of information gain evaluates whether an intermediate token segment helps improve the accuracy of the eventual answer.

This formulation leads to Meta Reinforcement Finetuning, or MRT, a class of methods that rewards useful intermediate progress alongside final correctness. On AIME, fine-tuning with MRT substantially improves both performance and token efficiency. The findings support training models to value the contribution of intermediate reasoning steps when the objective is to make additional test-time computation more productive.
icml-2025-optimizing-test-time-compute-v.tldr: MRT rewards intermediate information gain alongside final correctness to improve reasoning performance and token efficiency on AIME.

paragraphs: Protein sequence and three-dimensional structure depend on one another, so generating them coherently is a central design challenge. Pallatom approaches their joint distribution through an all-atom representation. Its aim is to generate protein structures with coordinates for all atoms while accounting for the relationship between sequence and conformation.

The model uses two representational tracks: one at the token level and another at the atomic level. A multilayer decoder integrates these through traversing representations and a recycling mechanism. The authors also introduce an atom14 representation to give unknown side-chain coordinates a unified description. This representation is designed to maintain fidelity between the generated atomic conformation and its physical structure.

Experiments report significant improvements in designability, diversity, and novelty, alongside improved generation accuracy and strong sampling efficiency. These findings support all-atom modeling as a productive way to couple sequence and structure during protein generation. The authors also identify larger and more complex systems as a direction for future application, building on the model’s reported efficiency.
icml-2025-p-all-atom-is-unlocking-new-pa.tldr: Pallatom models proteins through all-atom representations to jointly capture sequence and structure, improving reported protein design metrics and sampling efficiency.

paragraphs: Generating molecules for a protein target requires coordinating continuous three-dimensional positions with discrete molecular topology. These two forms of information jointly determine molecular geometry, but their probability paths can be difficult to coordinate during generation. This paper identifies the noise schedules governing those paths as an important design choice.

The authors establish that the schedules determine the variational lower bound associated with this coupled probability path. They then introduce VLB-Optimal Scheduling, which optimizes that bound as an integral along the path. The method makes the evolution of the different modalities part of the optimization, with the goal of improving both molecular geometry and interaction modeling.

On CrossDock, the model achieves a reported state-of-the-art PoseBusters passing rate of 95.9%, improving by more than 10% over strong baselines. The authors also report maintained high affinities and robust intramolecular validity on a held-out test set. These findings connect a change in generative scheduling to better geometric outcomes while retaining other evaluated qualities relevant to structure-based molecular design.
icml-2025-piloting-structure-based-drug-.tldr: VLB-Optimal Scheduling coordinates molecular generation modalities and achieves a 95.9% PoseBusters passing rate on CrossDock.

paragraphs: Explaining a molecular graph model becomes more complicated when it uses three-dimensional geometry. In these models, a distance cutoff can create many implicit connections between nearby atoms. Explanation methods focused on two-dimensional molecular substructures therefore do not directly address all the spatial relationships used by a 3D graph neural network.

RISE builds explanations around localized regions in three-dimensional space. Each node receives a radius of influence that defines the neighborhood included in its explanatory subgraph. Within that region, message passing represents the spatial and structural interactions relevant to the model’s prediction. The explanation is thus organized around the geometry that the model uses to exchange information.

The approach is intended to make predictions more interpretable by constraining explanations to local spatial neighborhoods. It also aligns the extracted subgraphs with physical and structural dependencies characteristic of molecular applications. The paper’s stated contribution is this geometry-aware explanation mechanism: it makes spatial extent an explicit part of identifying which portion of a molecular graph matters to a prediction.
icml-2025-rise-radius-of-influence-based.tldr: RISE explains 3D molecular graph predictions through localized subgraphs defined by a radius of influence around each node.

paragraphs: Max-k-Cut is a discrete graph optimization problem, and continuous relaxations are a common way to make it easier to optimize. A key difficulty is connecting the relaxed answer back to a good solution of the original problem. ROS organizes that process into three stages: relax the constraints, optimize the relaxed objective, and sample a discrete solution.

The relaxation represents discrete choices as points on a probability simplex. A graph neural network is pretrained and fine-tuned to optimize this continuous problem. A sampling-based construction then converts the result back into a Max-k-Cut solution. Combining geometric analysis with statistical theory, the authors establish consistency between the function values of the continuous solution and its mapped counterpart.

Experiments on random regular graphs and Gset report better performance than state-of-the-art algorithms, including instances with up to 20,000 nodes solved in a few seconds. ROS also generalizes across tested in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances. The contribution combines empirical scalability with a theoretical connection between the relaxed objective and the resulting discrete solution’s value.
icml-2025-ros-a-gnn-based-relax-optimize.tldr: ROS combines continuous relaxation, graph neural network optimization, and sampling to produce scalable Max-k-Cut solutions with function-value consistency.

paragraphs: Models of different sizes can appear to follow different training trajectories when their losses are plotted against raw compute. This paper finds a shared pattern for compute-optimally trained models: after scaling both compute and loss so that their final values equal one, the curves align onto a common trajectory.

With learning rate decay, this alignment becomes especially precise. Differences between normalized curves from different model sizes fall below the variation caused by random seeds within individual curves. The authors call this supercollapse and observe it across learning rate schedules, datasets, and architectures, including next-token prediction transformers. The pattern breaks down when hyperparameters are scaled suboptimally, making it a practical diagnostic of scaling quality.

The paper connects curve collapse to the power-law structure of neural scaling laws. It also analyzes a simple model of stochastic gradient descent noise that predicts loss curves across learning rate schedules and quantitatively explains supercollapse. These results link an empirical regularity in training to a compact account of optimization dynamics, with compute-optimal scaling central to the observed behavior.
icml-2025-scaling-collapse-reveals-unive.tldr: Compute-optimally trained models exhibit tightly aligned normalized loss curves, offering a diagnostic of scaling quality and a window into training dynamics.

paragraphs: Tabular in-context learning predicts from a table by placing labeled training examples in context, without updating model parameters for the new dataset. This approach can be computationally demanding on large tables. TabICL addresses that scaling problem for classification, targeting settings beyond the roughly 10,000-sample range where the abstract describes TabPFNv2 as particularly effective.

Its architecture separates representation building from in-context prediction. Column-then-row attention first converts rows into fixed-dimensional embeddings. A subsequent transformer performs in-context learning on those representations. TabICL is pretrained on synthetic datasets containing up to 60,000 samples, and the authors report that it can handle 500,000 samples using affordable resources.

Across 200 TALENT classification datasets, TabICL matches TabPFNv2 overall while running systematically faster, with speedups reaching tenfold, and significantly outperforms the other evaluated approaches. On 53 datasets exceeding 10,000 samples, it surpasses both TabPFNv2 and CatBoost. The results support the architectural separation as a way to extend in-context classification to larger tables while retaining competitive predictive performance.
icml-2025-tabicl-a-tabular-foundation-mo.tldr: TabICL scales in-context tabular classification through a two-stage architecture, delivering competitive accuracy and faster inference on large datasets.

paragraphs: Online conformal prediction seeks reliable coverage as predictions and outcomes arrive sequentially. Many algorithms resemble online gradient descent, but their worst-case coverage guarantees do not follow directly from its usual regret guarantee. This paper clarifies when no-regret learning does, and does not, establish the desired coverage properties.

Standard regret guarantees imply marginal coverage for independent, identically distributed data. The authors show that this implication fails in adversarial environments or when coverage is required within groups. They then establish a tight connection between threshold-calibrated coverage and swap-regret in adversarial settings. That connection extends to group-conditional, or multi-valid, coverage, linking a more specific learning guarantee to stronger coverage requirements.

The authors also show that follow-the-regularized-leader algorithms, a family including online gradient descent, can provide adversarial group-conditional coverage for arbitrary grouping functions. They use this relationship to analyze and experimentally evaluate a multi-group version of ACI. The contribution distinguishes what ordinary regret guarantees establish from what additional structure can deliver, helping explain why similar-looking algorithms need different coverage analyses.
icml-2025-the-relationship-between-no-re.tldr: The paper identifies where standard regret fails to imply coverage and connects stronger online learning structure to adversarial and group-conditional conformal guarantees.

paragraphs: De novo peptide sequencing infers peptide sequences from mass spectrometry data, where complex signals and uneven noise can create data-specific biases. RankNovo addresses this by reranking candidate sequences from multiple sequencing models. It aims to exploit their complementary strengths through a shared comparison step.

The framework evaluates a list of candidates together, representing them as a multiple sequence alignment. Axial attention extracts information across candidates to inform their ranking. The authors also introduce Peptide Mass Deviation and Residual Mass Deviation, which quantify mass differences at the whole-sequence and residue levels. These measures supply detailed supervision for learning which candidate sequences should receive higher ranks.

Experiments show that RankNovo surpasses the base models whose outputs supplied its pretraining candidates and establishes a new state of the art in the evaluated setting. It also generalizes in zero-shot tests to outputs from models absent during training. That transfer supports its potential as a broadly reusable reranker, allowing improvements to candidate selection to extend beyond the particular sequencing models used to train it.
icml-2025-universal-biological-sequence-.tldr: RankNovo improves peptide sequencing by jointly reranking candidates from multiple models and generalizes to outputs from unseen models.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution must balance faithfulness to a low-resolution input with realistic generated detail, while keeping computation manageable. VARSR tackles this using visual autoregressive modeling in which generation predicts the next image scale. This applies autoregressive generation to a progression of spatial resolutions.

Several components connect that progression to the original image. Prefix tokens carry the low-resolution conditioning information, while scale-aligned rotary positional encodings represent spatial structure across scales. A diffusion refiner models residual error from quantization to improve pixel-level fidelity. Image-based classifier-free guidance encourages realism, and the authors collect large-scale training data and design a training process to build robust generative priors.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show high-fidelity, realistic outputs with greater efficiency than diffusion-based methods in the reported comparisons. The approach gives different components complementary roles: next-scale prediction handles generation, conditioning preserves input semantics, and refinement addresses remaining pixel-level error. The findings support this combination as a way to improve the balance between visual quality and computation in super-resolution.
icml-2025-visual-autoregressive-modeling.tldr: VARSR combines next-scale autoregressive generation with conditioning and diffusion refinement for efficient, faithful, and realistic image super-resolution.

paragraphs: Image corruption from damaged imaging systems or difficult environments can undermine recognition models trained on clean images. Restoring inputs or adapting models can struggle with unknown corruption and may reduce clean-image accuracy. YARM investigates another intervention: designing an object’s appearance so that models can recognize it more reliably when the resulting images are degraded.

Inspired by warning colors and camouflage, the method synthesizes robust appearances for recognition under corruption across views. The authors show that certain features in radiance fields transfer between objects belonging to the same class even when their geometries differ. They also study how the proxy model used during appearance design affects transferability to other recognition models.

Experiments report better performance than image restoration and model fine-tuning approaches across several settings. The generated appearances also remain effective when transferred to models with different architectures. These findings support appearance design as a useful intervention for robust recognition, with demonstrated transfer across both same-class object geometries and model architectures in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-you-always-recognize-me-yarm-r.tldr: YARM designs object appearances that improve recognition under image corruption and transfer across tested geometries and model architectures.
